To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) a complete antiemetic response is the primary endpoint for assessing antiemetic therapy, and this should be evaluated by measuring both emesis and nausea; (2) new antiemetic drugs should be evaluated in a progression from open-label trials to randomized, placebo-controlled trials; and (3) a classification system for chemotherapy-induced nausea and emesis is proposed that incorporates the known patient- and treatment- related prognostic factors.

(1) the most important prognostic variables for emesis are age, gender and type of chemotherapy, (2) the most important antiemetic drug variables are dose and route of administration, and (3) the most important patient-related variable for nausea is gender.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a practical and useful methodology for evaluating antiemetics in the clinical setting.
the prevention and treatment of chemotherapy-induced nausea, vomiting and anticipatory nausea.
the development and evaluation of new antiemetic agents.

the antiemetic field has made significant progress in the past decade, and that the methodology of clinical antiemetic trials has been improved.

the antiemetic field has made significant advances in recent years, and that the methodology used in antiemetic trials has been refined.
